subtype: Stage 3: Routine and a core group [Observer]
passage:
I'm Francis, and I share a lab bench with Samir, so I see his group every day. There are five of them. They eat lunch at the same corner table in the canteen, near the water cooler, and nobody else sits there. Nobody was told not to; it's just understood. They study in the back room of the library, split cab fares home at Diwali, and have a group name I've never heard said aloud.
They look comfortable. Nobody has to plan who to sit with. Nobody eats alone.
But last month the debate club put up a poster, and Samir stood in front of it for a long time. When I asked if he'd join, he laughed and said, "The guys would think I've gone posh." He didn't sign up. Maybe he didn't want to. I can't tell. But he looked back at the poster twice on the way out.

qa.q: Where does Samir's group eat lunch?
qa.a: They eat lunch at the same corner table in the canteen, near the water cooler.

qa.q: What might Samir have been feeling in front of the debate poster?
qa.a: Samir may have wanted to join but worried the group would judge him; looking back twice suggests he was torn, though Francis can't be sure.

qa.q: What could Samir do if the group starts to feel limiting?
qa.a: Samir could try the debate club anyway and mention it lightly to the group; a secure friendship can stretch to make room for other interests.

qa.q: How does the group look to Francis from outside?
qa.a: To Francis the group looks comfortable and closed at once: nobody eats alone, yet nobody else sits at that table.

grounding: Shows an outsider watching a settled friend group that shares everything, with both real comfort and quiet pressure not to look beyond it.

subtype: Stage 3: Routine and a core group [Observer]
passage:
Week one: Arnab, new to the college after a transfer, noticed the four girls straight away. Gopika and her friends walked into Economics together, sat in the same row every day, and passed one flask of tea along it.
Week three: They'd been to Darjeeling together over the long weekend; the photos were on every phone in class. Arnab asked Gopika if she wanted to join his statistics study circle. She glanced at the others before answering, "Maybe, let me see." She didn't come.
Week six: Gopika came to the study circle alone, late, and sat near the door. She was quick with the formulas and helped two people. After an hour her phone buzzed four times. She read the messages, said, "They're waiting at the canteen," and left, apologising twice. Arnab wondered whether she'd wanted to stay.

qa.q: What did the group pass along their row in Economics?
qa.a: They passed one flask of tea along it.

qa.q: What might Gopika's glance at her friends suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Gopika felt she needed the group's okay, or worried how they would feel, before joining something outside it.

qa.q: What could help Gopika keep both her group and a new interest?
qa.a: Gopika could tell her friends plainly that she has the study circle for an hour and will meet them after, so the new commitment isn't treated as leaving.

qa.q: How does Arnab see Gopika's group over these weeks?
qa.a: Arnab sees warmth and closeness, but also a pull that brings Gopika back each time, and he wonders whether she wanted to stay.

grounding: Illustrates an outsider noticing over weeks how a close group's routines bring comfort and also an unspoken pull to stay inside it.
